{{Short description|Locally compact infinite topological field}}
In [[mathematics]], a '''local field''' is a [[locally compact]] [[Hausdorff space|Hausdorff]] non-[[Discrete space|discrete]] [[topological field]].{{sfn|Weil|1995|p=20}} Local fields find many applications in [[algebraic number theory]], where they arise naturally as [[Complete metric space#Completion|completions]] of [[global field]]s.{{sfn|Neukirch|1999|loc=Sec. 5|p=134}} Moreover, tools like [[Integral|integration]] and [[Fourier analysis]] are available for functions defined on local fields.

Given a local field, an [[Absolute value (algebra)|absolute value]] can be defined on it which gives rise to a [[Complete metric space|complete metric]] that generates its topology. There are two basic types of local field: those called '''Archimedean local fields''' in which the absolute value is [[Archimedean property#Definition for normed fields|Archimedean]], and those called '''non-Archimedean local fields''' in which it is not. Non-Archimedean local fields can also be defined as those fields which are complete with respect to a [[Metric space|metric]] induced by a [[discrete valuation]] whose [[residue field]] is finite.{{sfn|Cassels|Fröhlich|1967|loc=Ch. VI, Intro.|p=129}} 

Every local field is [[isomorphic]] (as a topological field) to one of the following:{{sfn|Milne|2020|loc=Remark 7.49|p=127}}

*Archimedean local fields ([[Characteristic (algebra)|characteristic]] zero): the [[real numbers]] <math>\R</math>, and the [[complex numbers]] <math>\C</math>.
*Non-Archimedean local fields of characteristic zero: [[finite extension]]s of the [[p-adic number|''p''-adic number]]s <math>\Q_p</math> (where <math>p</math> is any [[prime number]]).
*Non-Archimedean local fields of characteristic <math>p</math>: the field <math>\mathbb{F}_q((t))</math> of [[formal Laurent series]] in the variable <math>t</math> over a [[finite field]] <math>\mathbb{F}_q</math>, where <math>q</math> is a [[Exponentiation|power]] of <math>p</math>.

== Module, absolute value, metric ==
Given a local field <math>F</math>, a "module function" on <math>F</math> can be defined as follows. First, consider the [[Field (mathematics)#Related algebraic structures|additive group]] of the field. As a locally compact [[topological group]], it has a unique (up to positive scalar multiple) [[Haar measure]] <math>\mu</math>. The module of an element <math>a</math> of <math>F</math>  is defined so as to measure the change in size of a set after multiplying it by <math>a</math>. Specifically, define <math>\operatorname{mod}_K:F\to\R</math> by{{sfn|Weil|1995|p=4}}
:<math>\operatorname{mod}_K(a)=\frac{\mu(aX)}{\mu(X)}</math>
for any [[measurable]] subset <math>X</math> of <math>F</math> (with <math>0<\mu(X)<\infty</math>). This module does not depend on <math>X</math> nor on the choice of Haar measure <math>\mu</math> (since the same scalar multiple ambiguity will occur in both the numerator and the denominator). The function <math>\operatorname{mod}_K</math> is continuous and satisfies
:<math>\operatorname{mod}_K(ab)=\operatorname{mod}_K(a) \operatorname{mod}_K(b),</math>

:<math>\operatorname{mod}_K(a+b)\leq A\sup\left(\operatorname{mod}_K(a), \operatorname{mod}_K(b)\right)</math>
for some constant <math>A</math> that only depends on <math>F</math>. 

Using <math>\operatorname{mod}_K</math>, one may then define an absolute value <math>|\cdot|</math> on <math>F</math> that induces a [[Metric space|metric]] <math>d</math> on <math>F</math> (by setting <math>d(x,y)=|x-y|</math>), such that <math>F</math> is complete with respect to this metric, and the metric induces the given topology on <math>F</math>.

== Basic features of non-Archimedean local fields ==

For a non-Archimedean local field <math>F</math> with absolute value <math>|\cdot|</math>, the following objects are important:
*its '''[[ring of integers]]''' <math>\mathcal{O} = \{a\in F: |a|\leq 1\}</math> which is a [[discrete valuation ring]], is the closed [[unit ball]] of <math>F</math>, and is [[Compact space|compact]];

*the '''units''' in its ring of integers <math>\mathcal{O}^\times = \{a\in F: |a|= 1\}</math> which form a [[Group (mathematics)|group]] and is the [[unit sphere]] of <math>F</math>;

*the unique non-zero [[prime ideal]] <math>\mathfrak{m}=\{a\in F: |a|< 1\}</math> in its ring of integers, which is the open unit ball of <math>F</math>;

*a [[principal ideal|generator]] <math>\varpi</math> of <math>\mathfrak{m}</math> called a '''[[uniformizer]]''' of <math>F</math>; and

*its residue field <math>k=\mathcal{O}/\mathfrak{m}</math> which is finite (since it is compact and  [[Discrete space|discrete]]).

Every non-zero element <math>a</math> of <math>F</math> can be written as <math>a=\varpi^nu</math> with <math>u</math> a unit in <math>\mathcal{O}^\times</math>, and <math>n</math> a unique integer.
The '''normalized valuation''' of <math>F</math> is the [[surjective function]] <math>v:F\to\Z\cup\{\infty\}</math> defined by sending a non-zero <math>a</math> to the unique integer <math>n</math> such that <math>a=\varpi^nu</math> with <math>u</math> a unit, and by sending 0 to <math>\infty</math>. If <math>q</math> is the [[cardinality]] of the residue field, the absolute value on <math>F</math> induced by its structure as a local field is given by:{{sfn|Weil|1995|loc=Ch. I, Theorem 6}}
:<math>|a|=q^{-v(a)}.</math>

An equivalent and very important definition of a non-Archimedean local field is that it is a field that is [[complete valued field|complete with respect to a discrete valuation]] and whose residue field is finite.

=== Examples ===

*'''''p''-adic numbers''': the ring of integers of <math>\Q_p</math> is the ring of <math>p</math>-adic integers <math>\Z_p</math>. Its prime ideal is <math>p\Z_p</math> and its residue field is <math>\Z/p\Z</math>. Every non-zero element of <math>\Q_p</math> can be written as <math>up^n</math> where <math>u</math> is a unit in <math>\Z_p</math> and <math>n</math> is an integer, with <math>v(up^n)=n</math> for the normalized valuation.

*'''Formal Laurent series over a finite field''': the ring of integers of <math>\mathbb{F}_q((t))</math> is the ring of [[formal power series]] <math>\mathbb{F}_q[[t]]</math>. Its maximal ideal is <math>(t)</math> (i.e. the set of [[power series]] whose [[constant term]]s are zero) and its residue field is <math>\mathbb{F}_q</math>. Its normalized valuation is related to the (lower) degree of a formal Laurent series as follows:
::<math>v\biggl(\sum_{i=-m}^\infty a_iT^i\biggr) = -m</math>
:where <math>a_{-m}</math> is non-zero.

*The field <math>\C((t))</math> of formal Laurent series over the complex numbers is ''not'' a local field: its residue field is <math>\C((t))/(t)=\C</math>, which is not finite.

=== <span id="higherunit"></span><span id="principalunit"></span>Higher unit groups ===

The '''''n''-th higher unit group''' of a non-Archimedean local field <math>F</math> is
:<math>U^{(n)}=1+\mathfrak{m}^n=\left\{u\in\mathcal{O}^\times:u\equiv1\, (\mathrm{mod}\,\mathfrak{m}^n)\right\}</math>
for <math>n\geq 1</math>. The group <math>U^{(1)}</math> is called the '''group of principal units'''. The full unit group <math>\mathcal{O}^\times</math> is denoted <math>U^{(1)}</math>.

The higher unit groups form a decreasing [[filtration (mathematics)|filtration]] of the unit group
:<math>\mathcal{O}^\times\supseteq U^{(1)}\supseteq U^{(2)}\supseteq\cdots</math>
whose [[quotient group|quotients]] are given by
:<math>\mathcal{O}^\times/U^{(n)}\cong\left(\mathcal{O}/\mathfrak{m}^n\right)^\times\text{ and }\,U^{(n)}/U^{(n+1)}\approx\mathcal{O}/\mathfrak{m}</math>
for <math>n\geq 1</math>.{{sfn|Neukirch|1999|p=122}} (Here "<math>\approx</math>" means a non-canonical isomorphism.)

=== Structure of the unit group ===

The multiplicative group of non-zero elements of a non-Archimedean local field <math>F</math> is isomorphic to
:<math>F^\times\cong(\varpi)\times\mu_{q-1}\times U^{(1)}</math>
where <math>q</math> is the order of the residue field, and <math>\mu_{q-1}</math> is the group of (<math>q-1</math>)-st roots of unity in <math>F</math>. Its structure as an abelian group depends on its [[characteristic (algebra)|characteristic]]:
*If <math>F</math> has characteristic <math>p</math>, then
::<math>F^\times\cong\Z\oplus\Z/{(q-1)}\oplus\Z_p^\N</math>
:where <math>\N</math> denotes the [[natural number]]s;
*If <math>F</math> has characteristic zero, i.e. it is a finite extension of <math>\Q_p</math> of degree <math>d</math>, then
::<math>F^\times\cong\Z\oplus\Z/(q-1)\oplus\Z/p^a\oplus\Z_p^d</math>
:where <math>a\geq 0</math> is defined so that the group of <math>p</math>-power roots of unity in <math>F</math> is <math>\mu_{p^a}</math>.{{sfn|Neukirch|1999|loc=Theorem II.5.7}}

== Theory of local fields ==
This theory includes the study of types of local fields, extensions of local fields using [[Hensel's lemma]], [[Galois extension]]s of local fields, [[ramification group]]s, filtrations of [[Galois group]]s of local fields, the behavior of the norm map on local fields, the local reciprocity homomorphism and existence theorem in [[local class field theory]], [[local Langlands correspondence]], [[Hodge-Tate theory]] (also called [[p-adic Hodge theory|''p''-adic Hodge theory]]), explicit formulas for the [[Hilbert symbol]] in local class field theory.{{sfn|Fesenko|Vostokov|2002|loc=Chapters 1-4, 7}}

== Variant definitions ==
The definition for "local field" adopted in this article, as a locally compact Hausdorff non-discrete topological field, is common today. Some authors however reserve the term "local field" for what we have called "non-Archimedean local field". 

Research papers in modern number theory often consider a more general notion of non-Archimedean local field, requiring only that they be complete with respect to a [[discrete valuation]] and that the residue field be [[Perfect field|perfect]] of positive characteristic, not necessarily finite.{{sfn|Fesenko|Vostokov|2002|loc=Def. 1.4.6}} 

In his book ''[[Local Fields]]'', Serre defines "local fields" as fields that are complete with respect to a discrete valuation, without any restriction on the residue field, leading to a notion that is more general still.{{sfn|Serre|1979}}

== Higher-dimensional local fields ==
{{main|Higher local field}}
A local field is sometimes called a ''one-dimensional local field''.

A non-Archimedean local field can be viewed as the field of fractions of the completion of the [[local ring]] of a one-dimensional arithmetic scheme of rank 1 at its non-singular point.

For a [[non-negative integer]] <math>n</math>, an <math>n</math>-dimensional local field is a complete discrete valuation field whose residue field is an <math>(n-1)</math>-dimensional local field.{{sfn|Fesenko|Vostokov|2002|loc=Def. 1.4.6}} Depending on the definition of local field, a ''zero-dimensional local field'' is then either a finite field (with the definition used in this article), or a [[perfect field]] of positive characteristic.

From the geometric point of view, <math>n</math>-dimensional local fields with last finite residue field are naturally associated to a complete [[flag (geometry)|flag]] of subschemes of an <math>n</math>-dimensional [[arithmetic scheme]].
